utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Just to keep matters short, I establish that in the courtroom appeared Ms. Brehmeier-Metz and Mr. Groome for the Prosecution. You, Mr. Jordash, for the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. And you, Mr. Jovanovic, for the Defence of Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Simatovic is present as well; Mr. Stanisic is not present. Today a report was filed signed by the assistant commanding officer of the UNDU, Mr. Hansen, reporting on what he observed in his communication with Mr. Stanisic. Most important parts that Mr. Stanisic indicated that he feels too unwell to attend court in person, that he was not willing to waive his right to attend court in person, and that he did not express a wish to use the video conference link which is available to him. Then we have a document, "Absence From Court Due to Illness," which was signed by Mr. Stanisic in which he expresses that he is unable to attend court proceedings due to illness, that he has discussed the matter with his counsel, and he did not fill in the box that he understands that he has a right to be present at all trial proceedings and that he, however, waives that right, he has not ticked that box. Further we have just the second page of the absence in court which was filled in and signed by Dr. Eekhof and we also have received a report from Dr. Eekhof dated the 10th of June, 2009, addressed to the Registrar of the ICTY. And if I would summarise that report it would be that it's -- the situation seems to be unchanged in essence. Once we had received this report the Chamber staff has inquired with the parties whether there would be any questions to be put to Dr. Eekhof. The parties expressed that they would have no questions for Dr. Eekhof, and therefore the Chamber thought that it was not necessary, having no questions itself, that Dr. Eekhof should be on standby. Any comments in relation to this? Not Mr. Groome, not by the Stanisic Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not by you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that it will proceed in the absence of Mr. Stanisic for the same reasons as were applicable yesterday and which the parties will receive in writing. The situation being unchanged, the decision is the same as well. Whereas yesterday the decision of the Chamber may have come more or less as a surprise to Mr. Stanisic, in which case we granted him 15 minutes to see whether he still wanted to join the videolink. Today it's different. Mr. Stanisic could expect a similar decision of the Chamber, and where he expressed already that he would not want to use the videolink facilities, there's no reason to adjourn again and to send him this message and to give him an opportunity that's ... Mr. Jordash, I take it that you consider that a fair conclusion, apart from what you think about the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will proceed. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I turn the mike over to Ms. Brehmeier-Metz, I wanted to say that the technical problem has been resolved, so we will be playing the videos and the sound. I would like to express my gratitude to Dragan Randelovic who remained late last evening to correct the problem with the equipment. We've also distributed digital versions of the presentation so the Chamber and the Defence can look at some of the slides and the videos that were malfunctioning yesterday, and look at your own convenience. And with that, Your Honour, I would ask Ms. Brehmeier-Metz to continue her opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have the booths been provided with hard copies of any spoken word in any of the videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were provided with the slides -- so the transcript of the spoken word is on the slide. They have the hard copy of that, they'll have e-court, and they have the full text of our presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that often there is an English translation of the word spoken on the slide or on the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it is the task of our interpreters to translate for us what is said in the original language and not to repeat what someone else may have translated unless these are CLSS translations which meet the standards of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the videos have the original speaker speaking in B/C/S, so I'm assuming that that won't be translated. That will go out as it is. And for the English channel, the translation of that is there for the translator to see. So I don't believe there's any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but who made those translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Some are CLSS and some are draft translations of that text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we work on the basis of CLSS interpretation and translations. Now I take it that the interpreters would have no problems with the work of their colleagues having provided translations because the same standard of quality applies. If, however, there are any -- any draft translations, then I think it's appropriate that our interpreters would have the original language before them, and I think yesterday I specifically asked for hard copies of any transcript to be available so that, as I said yesterday, the interpreters -- that one has an opportunity to verify whether the words spoken are the same as the words written down, the transcript of the original -- originally spoken words; and that the other interpreter can then translate from that transcript. I would not -- some hesitation to ask them to do anything else than what they're supposed to do, that is, to translate the originally spoken words or to interpret them for us so that we have them originally spoken on the video and audio, and that we have verified translation into English and verified translation in French on the record. I think I invited you yesterday to provide hard copies of -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, you did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I have some difficulties in understanding why what was valid yesterday is not valid today anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. My focus was on trying to resolve a pretty significant technical problem. Your Honour, there is one clip of Mr. Seselj where there is the translation on the clip. Perhaps I could check before it's played whether it's -- it may be one of the CLSS translations. It was played and it's been in the possession of the Defence for over a year. I don't believe there's been any dispute about the accuracy of the translation. But certainly if Your Honour's is that it's CLSS, I will try to verify that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we rely on and that's what we are so happy with, the quality of our interpretation. Then let's get started. Let's see whether -- if there's any need to have a further transcript, whether you can provide it. And if not, we'll try to find a solution. My concern was not primarily whether the Defence had it but of course the completeness of the record is also for purposes of, for example, an appeal if ever an appeal would be there. It's for the Appeals Chamber to have complete information. Please proceed. Ms. Brehmeier-Metz, you will continue where you left us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: I will indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yesterday afternoon I finished off introducing the legal theory of the Prosecution case in relation to incidents charged in the SAO Krajina. The second region in Croatia covered by this indictment is Eastern Slavonia. The Serb Democratic Party or SDS had been established in Slavonia in 1990. As in other regions in Croatia, tensions rose in Slavonia throughout 1990 -- I apologise, in Slavonia throughout 1990, and in January 1991 the Serb National Council, or SNC, of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, which we will from now on refer to by its abbreviation SBWS, was established. The SNC proclaimed the Serbs in Croatia to be a sovereign people with a right to autonomy in February 1991. The area is depicted on slide number 55. At a meeting held at Backa Palanka just across the Danube river in Serbia, representatives of all the Serb villages in the SBWS formed the so-called Great National Assembly of SBWS. On 25th June, 1991, the very day that Croatia and Slovenia declared their respective independence this Great National Assembly declared secession from Croatia and established the Serb Autonomous Region or SAO SBWS. Goran Hadzic who had been the president of the Serbian National Council was elected prime minister designate. The SAO Western Slavonia was established in August 1991. This entity, however, will not play a prominent role in the proceedings before this Court. Suffice it to say that in February 1992, the SAO Western Slavonia along with the SAO SBWS joined the SAO Krajina and created the Republic of Serb Krajina. Goran Hadzic, who is depicted in slide 56, turned out to be the most prominent political figure in the self-proclaimed SAO SBWS. He had been a founding member and president of the Serbian National Council and was elected first prime minister designate and on 25th September 1991 prime minister of the SAO SBWS. When the three SAOs in Croatia merged into the RSK in February 1992, he became president of this newly built entity and remained in that position until December 1993 when Milan Martic took over. Like the political figures in the Krajina, the leadership of the newly created SAO SBWS would also refrain from doing anything without first consulting with Belgrade. Hadzic would regularly travel there to meet with both Slobodan Milosevic and Jovica Stanisic. He would receive instructions on how to proceed. When he came back to Dalj, he would convene the police and TO commanders and he would frequently mention things he was told by Milosevic. During an intercepted telephone conversation with Karadzic on 14th December 1991, Stanisic would say, among others: "I barely convinced Hadzic not to go ..." Thereby again indicating his close connection with the political leadership of SAO SBWS. Like the Krajina, the SAO SBWS also lacked money and resources, and the Government of Serbia provided the region with everything that was needed to support them. During his regular meetings with Jovica Stanisic, Hadzic would continuously address the question of equipping his police force and Stanisic would see that it would be provided. Jovica Stanisic, however, not only exerted his influence during meetings with Hadzic in Belgrade or other places in Serbia. He also personally came to Eastern Slavonia. Around 19th or 20th September, 1991, he arrived in Dalj. We will present evidence that Stanisic screamed at people and berated them because Vukovar, the town that then lay under siege by the JNA, had not surrendered yet. The witness will recall that Stanisic pointed out that they had all the equipment necessary to take the city. He ordered Hadzic to be brought to a meeting in Dalj together with all the TO commanders. Indeed, that meeting took place with Stanisic, Hadzic, and others being present. And in October 1991, as can be seen from slide 57, Stanisic came to see General Arandjelovic accompanied by two members of the Red Berets, Bozovic and Ivanovic, Crnogorac. The person to organise this was Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza, a member of the Serbian MUP who later became deputy minister of interior of the Republic of Serbia. Slide number 58 summarises what we know about him. Stojicic had been the head of the Anti-terrorist Unit, or SAJ, in the MUP Serbia since the late 1980s. He came to SAO SBWS by the end of September 1991, after Jovica Stanisic had come to Dalj and complained about Vukovar. We will invite you to draw the inference that although according to the organisation structure of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, Stojicic was not Stanisic's subordinate. He was sent by Stanisic in order to ensure that the local police forces would function according to the wishes of the leadership and in order to assist the furtherance of the JCE's common plan, which included the fall of Vukovar. Consequently, Stojicic, a member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, was appointed the commander of the SAO SBWS TO in early autumn 1991. Here on slide 59 we have some photos taken at Stojicic's funeral. We can see Milosevic and Arkan standing close to each other paying their respects, and the right frame of the slide shows Jovica Stanisic also present during the same occasion. Another member of the Serbian MUP who came to be of importance in the SAO SBWS was Radoslav Kostic, also known as Kola or Ante. Kostic had been an agent for the DB from early 1991 onwards. On slide number 60 you see another excerpt from the video taken at Kula in 1997 at the training centre that was named after Radoslav Kostic. Jovica Stanisic pays tribute to his comrade by laying down a wreath at Kostic's memorial. The Serbian DB had been involved in transporting weapons from the JNA barracks at Bubanj Potok, south of Belgrade, to Borovo Selo as early as April 1991. Kostic would oversee the transport of weapons. We will present evidence that huge quantities were arriving from Serbia in the region in June 1991. The weapons belonged to the JNA and the deliveries were organised by the Novi Sad DB with Kostic in charge. Kostic was also involved in forming the SAO SBWS milicija and oversaw their equipment with weapons through the Novi Sad DB. In September 1991, he accompanied Jovica Stanisic to Dalj. Slide 61 shows the amount of financial support that came from Serbia. It deserves to be noted that it was acknowledged that all this did not have any legal foundations and that one planned to continue to provide assistance nevertheless. Another intermediary between the political leadership in SAO SBWS and Belgrade was perhaps the most notorious paramilitary leader during the whole war: Zeljko Raznjatovic, or Arkan. He had begun his career in the 1980s, committing several serious crimes throughout Europe. Arkan had been a fervent supporter of the Belgrade soccer club Red Star Belgrade and had assembled a large group of violent hooligans around him. In 1990, using members of this group, he set up a paramilitary unit called Serbian Volunteer Guard or more notoriously, Arkan's men with its elite subunit, Arkan's Tigers. It was this group that would come to terrorise the non-Serb civilians in SAO SBWS and later in Bosnia. Arkan openly advocated the commission of war crimes to the men he trained. His second in command was another person who was already introduced: Milorad Ulemek, Legija. They would serve as a shock force, the strike force for the JNA that preferred that some of the more blatantly illegal crimes perpetrated against the population be committed by people like Arkan. Arkan had a very close working relationship with the Serbian MUP. His unit was supplied by the MUP and he would claim he would do nothing without Jovica Stanisic's knowledge and orders. A few days after the take-over of Dalj, Arkan came to Borovo Selo with some of his men, introduced them as being from the Serbian DB, and showed his ID card, which was a Serbian DB identity card. Many members of Arkan's Tigers would eventually be transferred to the Special Unit of the Serbian DB, the Red Berets or the JATD, Unit for Anti-terrorist Operations, and would receive payments directly from the DB. Slide 64 shows one of these lists, covering the time-period 16th to 31st December, 1994, and naming well-known members of Arkan's Tigers such as Milorad Ulemek, Legija; Rade Rakonjac, listed as number 3; Jugoslav Gluscevic, number 13; and Vlado Vukotic, number 31. I have redacted a portion of these payment records because they contain the names of protected witnesses who will testify before you. These records will also serve as corroboration of their evidence. Slide number 65 has at the bottom of it an excerpt from a report detailing the type of training that was being conducted in the training centres of the Special Units of the Serbian DB. I would also like to play a short clip in which Arkan, speaking in English, describes his unit's policy toward captured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: "Mr. Raznjatovic: We don't take any more prisoners. We're going to kill every fascist soldier we catch."

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: There are other military reports such as the one in slide number 66 that the Prosecution will tender that show the notoriety of Arkan for brutality and criminal conduct that was not only known by the non-Serbs who fled in terror at the sound of his name, but also the JNA, Serb politicians, and most importantly for the purposes of this case, to Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. In all, the SAO SBWS was never an independent entity. You will hear evidence that Slobodan Milosevic controlled Hadzic through Arkan and Stojicic, and Jovica Stanisic was the link between them and Belgrade. Since late 1990, many former members of the milicija, that is, the police forces, had left their office and had established their own milicija groups which operated independently and without any legal bases. In July 1991, Goran Hadzic, along with Radoslav Kostic tried to organise them. Kostic would remain the contact person for the milicija and supply them with what was needed. In the course of time, however, it became evident that Arkan had become so powerful in Erdut and Dalj that those men in the milicija who did not take side with him would endanger their lives. There were many who rather joined Arkan in the crimes that were later committed in the area. Around the summer of 1991, Hadzic set up a Special Unit that was initially meant to ensure his security. Eventually, this unit was renamed into the Serbian National Security, or SNB, and became a Special Unit with specific powers. It was meant to be the equivalent to the Special Units of the Serbian DB. Goran Hadzic was in overall command. Among those that were of importance within the SNB was Mihajlo Ulemek, Legija's uncle. He, as a member of Arkan's Tigers, was the head of security within the SNB. The SNB, however, did not only serve as security guards for the government. In the course of this trial we will present evidence that will show how the SNB, together with the local TOs, the milicija, and first and foremost Arkan's men were involved in the grave crimes that were committed in the region during the late 1991 and early 1992. In August 1991, Arkan set up a training centre in Erdut that was used not only to train members of his paramilitary group, but also volunteers and TO members. The training centre was well equipped. A report of late October 1991 mentions "large quantities of different infantry weapons, grenade launchers, hand-grenades, Zolja hand-held launchers, et cetera, that Arkan is issuing to whomever he wants." Arkan's, however, was not the only training centre in the region. In December 1991, the DB set up its own training centre near Ilok, just across the border from Backa Palanka. This training centre, which sometimes will also be referred to as Pajzos, served as one of the training camps of the DB for both Red Berets and volunteers. And it was specifically mentioned in Franko Simatovic's speech in Kula in 1997. Crnogorac was in charge of the camp, with Franko Simatovic paying regular visits to it. The Prosecution alleges Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic to be ultimately responsible for seven incidents in Erdut and Dalj between September 1991 and July 1992. As a result of these incidents, non-Serb civilians were forcibly removed from their lawful homes and a total of 107 persons were killed, merely because they were not of Serb ethnicity. Arkan's men and the local police set up makeshift detention centres where they would then hold non-Serb civilians under inhumane circumstances for the only reason of being non-Serb. They would constantly beat the detainees and threaten to kill them while they interrogated them. In the course of this opening the Prosecution will not describe all seven of these incidents; two of them may serve as examples as to how the events in SAO SBWS took place. The first incident that the accused are charged with occurred in mid-September 1991. Goran Hadzic himself brought a number of Croat civilians to the police headquarter in Dalj. For the detainees, life turned to be hell. Every night and also during the days some of them were taken out of the cells and beaten severely. You will hear the evidence of one of the detainees, who will describe to you that at one point a man kicked the door of the cell, broke the lock, and entered. He told the detainees, "I want you to know I am Arkan," and looked on while the three men accompanying him started beating the prisoners with iron chairs. Around the 23rd of September, 1991, Hadzic and Arkan came back to the detention centre in Dalj. Arkan was accompanied by some 20 of his Serbian Volunteer Guard. They selected two of the detained civilians and let them go. The remaining 11 detainees were then taken out of detention and killed by Arkan and his men. Immediately afterwards, the commander of Dalj police station, a Serb, reported the incident to the ministry. His report is shown on slide number 68. He was removed from his post on 1st October, 1991. On 9th November, 1991, members of the local TO, SAO SBWS MUP forces and members of Arkan's men arrested at least nine non-Serb civilians in and around Erdut and took them to the TO training centre in Erdut where they shot them dead the following day. Several days later, the widow of one of the men started to make inquiries about her husband. Mihajlo Ulemek intervened and ordered the execution of the rest of the family, whereupon members of the SNB and of Arkan's men arrested and killed the widow, her son, and his wife. Another widow of those men that were killed on 10th November asked for their whereabouts. On 3rd June, 1992, she was arrested by members of the SNB. They took her to Erdut, killed her, and threw the body in an abandoned well in Dalj Planina. It is the Prosecution's case, as summarised on slide 69, that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic participated in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove Croats and other non-Serbs from targeted lands in the SAO SBWS through organising, training, and financing the direct perpetrators of the crimes in Eastern Slavonia. They also contributed to this common plan by exerting a huge influence on and directing the SAO SBWS government, and in particular Goran Hadzic who would then order and direct the crimes that were committed. As we have seen, the storm that was intended to sweep away anything non-Serb began in the south of Croatia, the Krajina. From there it moved to Eastern Slavonia, where it reached its climax in late 1991. Serb forces would now turn their attention to the areas in Eastern Bosnia that lie on the border to Croatia and Serbia, and the first municipalities that would suffer would be Bijeljina and Zvornik. In order to understand how the joint criminal enterprise applied its programme in Bosnia, the Chamber has to recognise why Bosnia was unique among the six former republics of Yugoslavia, why it presented fundamentally different challenges to the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise's objectives, and why Bosnia tragically suffered some of the gravest crimes committed during the war. In the simplest terms, the characteristic which made Bosnia unique and which must be understood is that, unlike other former republics that had large minority populations that were relatively contiguous, Bosnia's pockets of large ethnic populations were disconnected, spread out across the country in a polka-dot pattern, some communities resembling ethnic islands in a sea dominated by some other ethnic groups. What historians and other observers rightly extolled as evidence of the peaceful integration of different ethnicities and cultures would prove to present a special problem for the members of the joint criminal enterprise. What plan did they decide upon to break up this large patchwork of ethnicities and carve out an area that would be dominated by Serbs? One articulation of their plan can be found in a document. Before describing that document and what happened in Bosnia, I would like to take a few minutes to speak about some of the central people involved in the crimes that occurred in Bosnia. Radovan Karadzic was the first president of the Bosnian Serb government which would eventually be called the Republika Srpska. As such, he had formal authority over the Bosnian Serb Army and the Bosnian Serb police. He has been indicted by this Tribunal and is currently awaiting trial. He made his intentions clear in a speech given on 15th October, 1999, which is before you in slide number 71.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people to possible extinction. Because Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here."

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: The Prosecution will establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: The Prosecution will establish with intercept evidence, documents, and testimony the interaction between Jovica Stanisic and Dr. Karadzic, who played a paramount role as a core member of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution will introduce a number of intercepts between Mr. Stanisic and Dr. Karadzic, mostly from the critical period of August 1991 until February 1992. In these conversations, you will hear them discuss both political and practical issues related to the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise's plans, and will understand that the two men realised that what they were discussing was covert and had to remain hidden because you will hear them talk on these intercepts in guarded language, at times even reminding each other of the importance of not saying too much on the phone. In an intercept of 14th December, 1991, Jovica Stanisic tells Radovan Karadzic that he will send his men over into Bosnia to deal with specific problems. Stanisic also refers to "his boys," whom he says he has sent in previously. And finally, Stanisic tells Dr. Karadzic that he will order Goran Hadzic, the Croatian Serb leader from Eastern Slavonia, to do something. Momcilo Krajisnik, shown here with Biljana Plavsic on slide number 72, was a member of the Bosnian Serb leadership during the war. He held a number of senior political positions, including being a member of the National Security Council, the Expanded Presidency of the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was also the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. He was convicted of persecutions as a crime against humanity. Biljana Plavsic was a leading Bosnian Serb politician from before the conflict until the war's end. She was notorious for the extremity of her Serb nationalist ideology. She was a member of the collective Presidency of Bosnia, a member of the three-member Presidency of the Serbian Republic, and was a member of the Supreme Command of the Bosnian Serb Army. After pleading guilty to the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity, she was sentenced to 11 years' imprisonment. Ratko Mladic was a career JNA officer who became chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He has been indicted by this Tribunal and is currently a fugitive. He said, and it is printed on slide number 73: "People and peoples are not pawns nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here to there. "We cannot cleanse nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that Serbs would fall through and the rest leave ... I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People, this would be genocide." A document that articulates the objective of Bosnian Serbs was officially introduced at the 16th Session of the Assembly of the so-called Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 12th May, 1992. It lays out six strategic objectives for the Bosnian Serb people. In Mr. Simatovic's speech in Kula, he tied the activities of the Special Units of the Serbian DB to those six objectives. The first objective, shown here on slide number 74, is the separation of the Serbian people from the other two national communities. Two: Establishment of a corridor between Semberija and the Krajina. Mr. Simatovic's remark at Kula that his units were involved in the "corridor at Brcko" is a reference to the second strategic objective, to connect lands the Serbs targeted in the western and eastern parts of Bosnia. Three, shown here on slide number 76: Establishment of a corridor in the Drina Valley, eliminating the Drina River as a boundary between Serbs. This corridor was really a large expanse of territory comprising most of the eastern half of Bosnia. Mr. Simatovic refers to his unit's presence in "the Drina." Slide number 77 shows the fourth strategic goal: Establishing a border on the Una and Neretva Rivers. Five: The division of Sarajevo. When Mr. Simatovic refers to operations in Sarajevo, he is referring to this objective. And six: The sixth strategic objective was providing the Serbs with access to the sea. As we describe the crimes committed in the six Bosnian municipalities in which the present indictment charges crimes, we ask the Chamber to keep in mind how the locations targeted by the accused and the crimes they perpetrated there advanced the objectives expressed in these goals. With respect to the joint criminal enterprise as it was applied to the unique geography and demography of Bosnia, these goals are clear articulations of the shared intent of the core members of the joint criminal enterprise. In December 1991 a document with the title: "Instructions for the Organisation and Activity of the Organs of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina in Extraordinary Circumstances" was promulgated among high level representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The document became more popularly known as the Variant A and B document because of its contents. When it prescribed the actions to be taken by SDS functionaries, it distinguished between municipalities in which the Serbs were the majority, this was Variant A; and those municipalities in which Serbs were in the minority, this was Variant B. In essence, the document contained precise instructions regarding how local Serbs were to convene and declare a local assembly of Serbian people in the municipality which would then take upon itself the authority to take over the functions of the existing government, including the function of the existing police and security structures. Municipal take-overs proceeded in four steps. The first step was the construction of a system of governance that paralleled the official government, but was for Serbs only; second, the arming of the Serb population; third, the violent armed take-over of non-Serb municipalities; and fourth, the ethnic cleansing, whether through murder or expulsion, of the non-Serb population. Here in slide number 80 is a map of the Special Unit's training facilities. The 13 labelled in yellow are camps that the accused established in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As you can see, they are in areas marked for Serbs by the second, third, and fourth strategic objectives; Eastern Bosnia along the Drina, northern Bosnia, the land bridge between Semberija in the Krajina, and southern Bosnia along the Una and Neretva Rivers. In this trial the Prosecution will confine its evidence to just six of the many municipalities that were taken over in this manner. These municipal areas are: (A) Bijeljina, in north-western Bosnia. Our evidence will be confined to the forcible transfer of people from that municipality; (B) Zvornik, the label for Zvornik is in the right-hand column, number six from both the bottom and the top; (C) Bosanski Samac, the label for Bosanski Samac is in the top row, far right; (D) Sanski Most, in north-central Bosnia. Later Mr. Groome will talk about the events in Sanski Most in 1995; (E) Doboj, the label for Doboj is in the top row, second from the left; (F) Trnovo, near Sarajevo, the Special Units were not involved in the take-over of this area, but in June and July of 1995, in the aftermath of Srebrenica one of the State Security Special Units, the Skorpions, participated in the execution that followed the fall of Srebrenica by summarily executing six Muslim males. The Special Units of the Serbian DB directly participated in the take-over of each of the other five municipal areas. After the violent take-over of these towns, non-Serbs, predominantly Muslims, were forcibly removed from their homes and their land through the commission of the crimes of murder and persecution, perpetrated with the intent to secure the area for Serbs. Many who were not killed were forced at gunpoint to sign over the property rights to their lands and then placed on a bus to take them out of the area. Others were subjected to unrelenting harassment and persecutory acts which took the form of arbitrary arrests, illegal detention in appalling conditions, beatings, curfews, and frequent, aggressively conducted searches of the homes of non-Serbs. Creating an ethnically pure Serb municipality in a peaceful, multi-ethnic community is hard to imagine in any case. It really stretches our capacity to imagine what such an enterprise would entail when we consider a place like the municipality of Zvornik, which prior to the war in 1991 had a population that was 54.8 per cent Muslim. After the war, 1997 or 1998, only 0.6 per cent of the population of Zvornik was Muslim. Mr. Groome will now summarise the evidence of five municipalities in Bosnia of which the Prosecution will lead evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brehmeier-Metz. Mr. Groome, please proceed, and keep in mind the speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I ask what time the Chamber would like to break so that I can be mindful of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually the first break is after one and a half hour, which would mean that since we had a late start that that would be in approximately 15 to 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, on the 24th of March, 1992, about eight days before the Bijeljina take-over, Radovan Karadzic stated, as shown in slide number 81, that soon the Serbian municipalities will begin the take-over process. The take-over of Bijeljina and Zvornik was a well-planned and well-executed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my learned friend from the Prosecution, but also with the previous speaker we were told that those were Bosnian municipalities and Bijeljina was the first one to be listed, but in the third amended indictment Bijeljina does not exist anymore, it has been excluded. So based on the third amended indictment, the Bosnian municipalities within the crime base are Bosanski Samac, Doboj, Sanski Most, Trnovo, and Zvornik. I don't think that we need to hear about the events in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, Mr. Jovanovic expresses his concerns as to whether in this opening statement you go beyond what is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Ms. Brehmeier-Metz stated, the Prosecution is still -- there are still counts in the indictment related to the forcible transfer of Muslims from Brioni. While it is true that in the third amended indictment the Prosecution did drop some of the individual counts of murder, it never dropped the forcible transfer. And it has always been the position of the Prosecution that the events of Bijeljina and Zvornik are so inextricably intertwined that the evidence which is led in Bijeljina is absolutely necessary to an understanding of what occurred in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, is there any dispute about the forcible transfer still being charged in relation to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could understand this if in the broader context of Zvornik the Prosecution speaks of Bijeljina as well; however, in the third amended indictment, Bijeljina has been excluded and all of the events which take -- took place there. It was included in the previous indictment but not in this one. So the events in Bijeljina have been completely dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it might assist, Mr. Jovanovic refers to paragraph 64 and 65 of the third amended indictment. Toward the bottom of both of those paragraphs, it will be clear that with respect to counts 4 and 5, deportation and inhumane acts, forcible transfers, that indeed Bijeljina is still very much a part of the Prosecution indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check it. Meanwhile please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the take-over of Bijeljina and Zvornik was a well-planned and well-executed campaign that occurred with precision and lightning speed over the course of a few days. The Special Units of the Serbian DB, in this case Arkan's men, established a camp in Serbia, just over the border from Bijeljina, poised to attack when given the signal in the early morning hours of the night of March 31st into the morning of the 1st of April, 1992. Both Bijeljina and Zvornik fell within the first and most important goal, the separation of the ethnic populations, as well as within the second and third strategic goals, the establishment of a corridor to areas targeted by Serbs that lie in central and Western Bosnia and the establishment of a Serb corridor in the Drina River Valley. In an effort to shorten the length of this trial, the Prosecution, as just discussed, will no longer seek to prove the killings and persecutions that occurred in Bijeljina. And while we will only prove the crimes against humanity of deportation and forcible transfer with respect to Bijeljina, a basic understanding of what happened there is essential in order for the Chamber to understand who Arkan was and what Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic knew about him. The brutality of Arkan in Bijeljina was even reported contemporaneously by senior officers in the Yugoslav Army, one of whom saw the awesome potential for unimaginable inter-ethnic crimes, as recorded here on slide number 83. In this contemporaneous report a major-general in the Yugoslav Army complains that movements of his own armoured units were restricted by Arkan and his men. Arkan and his 50 men could hold up a JNA armoured column because Arkan was a core member of the group of people who were behind these crimes. Shortly after the take-over of Bijeljina, we see Arkan and Mrs. Plavsic greet each other with a kiss here shown on slide 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be Bijeljina where Arkan would cement his reputation for unbridled brutality. Slide 85 shows two photos shot by Ron Haviv, a war photographer. He introduced the world to the brutality of Arkan's men. Shortly after the pictures shocked the world, Arkan himself identified the men in the picture as his to a BBC correspondent. As a result of the efforts of the joint criminal enterprise and relevant to the indictment now before the Chamber, many of the non-Serbs of Bijeljina were forced out or fled in terror. Your Honours, if there was a colourable claim that the two accused were unaware of Arkan's penchant for extreme violence before Bijeljina, there can be no escaping this knowledge after Bijeljina, as Arkan made his way to his next target: Zvornik. Zvornik is one of the towns that lie on the eastern border of Bosnia, separated from Serbia by the Drina River. Several bridges in the town connected it to Mali Zvornik, its sister town in Serbia. You will hear witnesses describe how in the weeks before the take-over of the town, JNA artillery positions were established in Mali Zvornik with guns pointing towards Bosnia. The take-overs of Bijeljina and Zvornik were the product of one well-planned operation. The Prosecution will introduce the transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation, shown here in slide 88, in which Plavsic speaks with Arkan's deputy and asks about how things went in Zvornik and asks him to pass on her request for Arkan to come to another municipality. A group of responsible local Serb and Muslim leaders from Zvornik tried tenaciously to keep the peace in Zvornik. During a meeting in which they had reached agreements that would have hopefully prevented violence, Arkan burst into the room, slapped the Serb representative, accusing them of giving away Serb lands. This is referred to on slide number 89. Arkan turned to the Muslim negotiator and gave him an ultimatum. It is in red at the bottom of the slide. Izet Mehinagic would recount these events in a desperate telegram to the Yugoslav People's Army, which is the text above the ultimatum on this slide. On the evening of the 8th of April the take-over was underway. The adult men were separated and at least 20 civilians murdered. Following the take-over, the surviving Muslims of Zvornik were subjected to a reign of terror. Reports like this one on slide number 90 and others we have seen show Arkan's effectiveness at achieving the joint criminal enterprise's goals. They also show notice to the JCE's core members of Arkan's ability to whip up Serbian nationalistic fervor. Kozluk was a small town on the outskirts of Zvornik. After the initial take-over, the predominantly Muslim population sought to reach a peaceful settlement with the Serbs now in power. But on the 26th of June, 1992, the Muslims of Kozluk were told to leave by the Serb mayor. Here is a list of those who were forced out on slide number 91. The mayor told the Muslims that if they did not leave, an all-out attack would be launched which would kill all the Muslims. The Muslims left, but not before Serb authorities made them sign papers giving their homes, land, and personal property to the new government in Zvornik. The deportees were taken along the route shown by the blue line toward Hungary on the map shown on slide number 92. When Hungarian authorities denied them entry because they did not have passports, the deportees were issued Serbian passports, that is, Bosnian nationals were issued with the passports of another country: Serbia. You will recall from yesterday's discussion of the mandate of Mr. Stanisic's department or Mr. Stanisic's ministry, that it included the control of passports. Vojislav Seselj was a core member of the joint criminal enterprise, president of the Serb Radical Party, who formed the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and sent his volunteers to conflict areas of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In a videotaped interview with the BBC, Vojislav Seselj would describe the involvement of Simatovic in the planning of the take-over of Zvornik. I will now ask that the video on slide number 94 be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Zvornik operation was planned in Belgrade too. Bosnian Serb forces participated in it and they were more numerous. However, the Special Units and the units most eager to fight came from this side. Those were the very police units, the so-called Red Berets, they are the Special Units of the Serbian State Security Service. "It was devised by the key people from the State Security Service, among them Franko Simatovic, Frenki. He was one of the direct perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, would that be -- would that be a convenient place to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Groome. How much time would you still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I certainly will finish within the next session, Your Honour. It's hard to judge the precise time, but I can say with confidence that it wouldn't take more than the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break and we'll resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Groome, I would like to invite perhaps at a later moment Ms. Brehmeier to explain to us in still number 61 what the billions of dinars are approximately in real money, because I couldn't gain any impression on how much money was really spent. And since I think the economy at that time was mainly done in Deutschemarks, perhaps if a translation into understandable currency could be made it would be appreciated. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just on that point, as it seems Your Honour is already aware, that was a period of significant hyper inflation where witnesses talk about the price of a quart of milk going up between the time they walked into the store and the time they went to pay for it, but we will make every effort to try to give an estimate of what it was in Deutschemarks. Your Honour, if I might return now to Zvornik. One of the reasons that Zvornik was one of the municipalities selected by the Prosecution is that it clearly demonstrates the intent that the members of the core group of perpetrators shared. The excesses perpetrated against the Muslim population of Zvornik had spiralled into a level of chaos in which no one, not even Serbs, were safe from the criminals turned loose with impunity in the municipality of Zvornik, as we can see in this report on slide number 95. In a report drafted by Colonel Tolimir about events all over Bosnia on the 28th of July, 1992, he raise the question with his superiors of the men who had perpetrated such grievous crimes in Zvornik with his superiors. Here in slide number 96 he identifies by name Arkan's men, Captain Dragan's men, and Seselj's men. He describes these three groups as being composed of many criminals, even pathological criminals. He states that these formations: "... display hatred of non-Serbian peoples and one can conclude without reservations that they are the genocidal element among the Serbian people." He goes on to say: "War profiteering and looting are the motive for a great majority of paramilitaries." Here on slide number 97 Tolimir enumerates the 30 to 40 million German marks' worth of booty stolen from the area of Srebrenica and Skelani. In the end of July 1992 there was a crack-down against paramilitary forces in Zvornik. In fact, the Serbian DB would itself be involved in the investigation of these paramilitary units. Two paramilitary leaders, the Vukovic brothers, leaders of the Yellow Wasps, would ultimately be investigated and arrested by the Serbian MUP. Your Honours, the two accused contributed to the goals of the JCE in the ways outlined in the box on the right-hand side of slide 98 and by so doing made themselves individually, criminally liable for the crimes committed in Zvornik. All elements of the JCE, except those from the Republic of Serb Krajina on the far left of the diagram, had some involvement in the take-over and ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina and Zvornik. Bosanski Samac, shown here on slide 99, located along the Sava River in north-Eastern Bosnia, had the misfortune of lying in the lands targeted to create the land bridge between land targeted by Serbs in the east of Bosnia and the land targeted by Serbs in the Krajina region. A successful conquest and ethnic cleansing of Bosanski Samac would achieve the first and second goals, namely, separation of the ethnic communities and establishment of a corridor, the Posavina corridor as it came to be popularly known. In early 1992 the Serb Crisis Staff of the Bosanski Samac municipality sent 20 local men to be trained in the Red Beret Training Camp in Ilok. These men were just completing their training at the Red Beret camp when the take-overs of Bijeljina and Zvornik were underway. They were airlifted back to Bosanski Samac on JNA helicopters with 30 members of Seselj's men. Before leaving, they were personally briefed by Mr. Simatovic. The day after Arkan announced he had finished his task in Zvornik the attack on Bosanski Samac commenced. Among these 50 men who went to Bosanski Samac, there were others who were trained by the Serbian DB who would work with them in the take-over of the town. Slobodan Miljkovic, also known as Lugar, was present; as were Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni; and Srecko Radovanovic, also known as Debeli; and a group of men from Serbia. As this report on slide 100 indicates, Crni, one of the leaders of the crimes perpetrated in Samac, was in fact arrested and what happened after his arrest demonstrates the role that both Simatovic and Stanisic played in the take-over of Samac. Another report shown here on slide 101 summarises the types of crimes that Crni and his men were believed to have perpetrated. They include specific allegations including murder and the looting of expensive cars. A local Serb leader recognising the loss of Crni to their efforts to ethnically cleanse Samac went to the Serbian MUP building in search of Franko Simatovic. It was his intention to ask Mr. Simatovic if there was anything he could do to secure Crni's release from the military police. He was unable to find Mr. Simatovic but as he walked in the parking-lot he by chance saw Jovica Stanisic, who he approached and explained the problem to. Mr. Stanisic told him that he would see to the matter by sending a telex to the military. Shortly thereafter Crni was released to continue his crimes. The answer to how Crni, a man whose excesses resulted in his arrest by the Bosnian Serb Army he was fighting alongside of, could promptly be released is perhaps best captured in a report issued by the local military authorities. In this document on slide 102 the author makes the observation that the crimes now being committed in the name of Serbs are comparable to the crimes committed against the Serbs in the Second World War. The basic facts of Crni's release were set out in this Bosnian police report on slide number 103. The Prosecution charges that the two accused contributed to the achievement of the JCE's goals in the ways listed in the box on the right of slide number 104. By doing so they made themselves individually criminally liable for the crimes committed in Bosanski Samac. As in Bijeljina and Zvornik, all elements of the JCE, except those in the Republic of Serb Krajina, were involved. Before the war, the population of Bosanski Samac had been 29.8 per cent Croat and 8.7 per cent Muslim. After the war those figures were 1.9 per cent Croatian and 1.3 per cent Muslim. Like Samac and Brcko, these municipalities not only had large non-Serb populations that needed to be removed, but they also lay in the corridor or land bridge that was to be created between the targeted lands in west of Bosnia and the targeted lands in the east. Over 15.000 Muslims would flee Doboj during the take-over. When the war began Doboj municipality was 30 per cent Muslim, 11 and a half per cent Croat, and 50 per cent Serb; by the war's end, it was 0.6 per cent Muslim, 1.5 per cent Croat, 92.5 per cent Serb. Before the take-over of Doboj men from a long list of DB paramilitaries began converging on Doboj including Martic's men from the Krajina. While Arkan commanded his own men and Seselj's men had their own commanders, the remaining men were referred to as Red Berets and were commanded by Rajo Bozovic, a colonel in the Special Units of the Serbian DB. The take-over of Doboj ended on the 3rd of May, 1992. This overwhelming force, many trained and outfitted by Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, were able to quickly and decisively seize control of a municipality with a population of 102.549 people covering an area of 684 square kilometres. When the town was firmly in Serb control, the campaign of persecutions against Doboj's Muslims began, mirroring what by this time had become the well-known signature of those units: Beatings, arbitrary arrests, interrogations, and murder. Non-Serb homes were aggressively searched and damaged, making it clear that non-Serb families who had lived in Doboj for generations had now better leave. Non-Serb civilians from Doboj were taken into custody and housed in various makeshift detention facilities in and around Doboj. For example, nearly 200 people were imprisoned in a disco. In these facilities the detainees were beaten and some prisoners were taken out and summarily executed. Muslim prisoners were forced to eat pork, in violation of their religious beliefs. In acts of almost unspeakable vulgarity prisoners were compelled to perform sexual acts upon each other. On the 12th of July, 1992, about 50 detainees were taken from the disco and used as human shields. These detainees were placed in front of the Serbian front lines and made to walk toward the front lines of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the detainees hesitated, a Serb shot one detainee in the head to encourage the others. When the Bosnian soldiers began beckoning the detainees, calling them to run towards the Bosnian front lines, the detainees broke into a run, the Serbs then opened fire killing 27 of these human shields. So decisive and absolute was the Red Berets' campaign in Doboj that those in the neighbouring municipality of Teslic would look to it as an example, as indicated in this report shown on slide number 106. The report mentions by name Bozovic, the same Bozovic who Milosevic recognises on the Kula tape. These are but four of the many municipal areas that were taken over by Bosnian Serbs in the spring and summer of 1992, take-overs that were marked by the precision of their execution and the brutality of their success. The Prosecution charges that the two accused contributed to the achievement of the JCE goals in the ways set out in the box on the right of slide 107, and by doing so incurred personal criminal liability for the crimes committed in Doboj. Here, different from the previous municipalities, it is also the Prosecution's case that the direct involvement of Martic's men also implicates the individual criminal responsibility of the accused. The overall criminal plan was a success and many municipalities were placed under Serb control in the spring of 1992. To place the crimes committed in these four municipalities in the context of the overall plan of the joint criminal enterprise, it is helpful to look at a series of maps on slides 108 to 115 that show in chronological order the take-over of territory as well as the role the two accused took in this process. It is the Prosecution's case that the rapid, comprehensive, and organised assertion of Serb control over territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina is evidence of the existence of and the effectiveness of the joint criminal enterprise. The take-over process begins when Arkan enters Bijeljina on the night between the 31st of March and the 1st of April. In that first week, over a dozen municipalities would be taken over and placed under Serb control. While some of those municipalities such as Titov Drvar were predominantly Serb and asserting control was primarily done by switching allegiance from Sarajevo to Pale. In other municipalities such as Bijeljina, these municipalities were taken by armed force and the commission of serious crimes against the civilian population. During the second week, the focus of the take-overs would remain on the Drina Valley and Serb take-overs swept over Eastern Bosnia in places like Visegrad, Foca, and Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As you have already heard, Mr. Stanisic and Simatovic played a direct role in the take-over of Zvornik and the expulsion of its large Muslim population. In Central Bosnia the municipality of Teslic fell during the second week of April. Here in slide 111 we see that in the third week of the take-over, after Arkan would advise that his work was completed in Zvornik, the Special Units of the Serbian DB would turn their attention to the municipality of Bosanski Samac. The take-overs continue along the Drina River with Bratunac and in Foca's neighbour to the west, Kalinovik, Vogosca, part of the greater Sarajevo area would also fall under Serb control this week. Up in the north-western part of Bosnia, in the Bosnian Krajina, Serb control would be forcibly imposed with its by now characteristic crimes in Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most. Serb gains would continue in the Bosnian Krajina into the last days of April when Prijedor, where some of the most grievous crimes of the take-overs were committed. Serb control was asserted over Mrkonjic Grad and large parts of Bosanska Krupa, bringing the border of Serb-controlled lands to the banks of the Una River. The campaign in the Drina Valley would continue with the take-over of Vlasenica and the encirclement of Sarajevo in preparation of its siege. By the end of April in this 30-day period, 35 municipalities would be taken over, an average of over one municipality per day. While the pace of the take-overs would slow a bit during the following months, the pace of the crimes only accelerated. The accused would send Colonel Bozovic, along with other members of the Special Units, to spear-head the take-over of Doboj, a critical municipality in the Posavina corridor. The encirclement around Sarajevo would be complete with the taking of Hadzici, Trnovo, and Ilidza in May. With the fall of Rogatica and Rudo, the take-over of the municipalities along the eastern border of Bosnia would be complete with the exception of Srebrenica. Also in May, three more municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina would also fall. The Bosnian Krajina would be completely secured by the end of June with the take-over of Prnjavor and Kotor Varos. During June the primary focus of take-overs shifted to the southern areas of Bosnia where Nevesinje, Bileca, and Ljubinje would be placed under Serb control as well as Trebinje with the exception of its southern area of Ravno which was controlled at the time by Croatian forces. By the end of the summer with the take-over of Derventa and Odzak, over 50 municipalities would be placed under Serb control to secure the functioning of the Posavina corridor. The two maps you now see on the screen in slide 116 are demographic maps; one from 1991, before the ethnic cleansing campaign of 1992; and one from 1997, after the campaign. You may observe by the success -- the success of the joint criminal enterprise as measured statistically in dramatic demographic changes. If you look along the Posavina corridor, that is the horizontal oval at the top of the map, the target of the second strategic goal, you will see a dramatic shift in the population as marked by the change of colour to red. The vertical oval on the right-hand side of the map is the Drina Valley, and again you can see the dramatic shift in colour represents the restructuring of the demographic landscape from mixed or Muslim majority municipalities into red, Serb municipalities. These take-overs and subsequent crimes resulted in population shift hundreds of thousands of people. Nearly 400.000 people forcibly removed from their homes. The map on slide 117 shows what happened after the summer of 1992. Some additional take-overs would continue. The light blue municipalities show where there will be evidence of involvement of the Special Units of the Serbian DB; and the dark blue municipalities indicate those locations in which the two accused are charged with the commission of crimes. The next charges in the indictment will concern the serious crimes committed toward the end of the conflict in 1995. It would be incorrect for the Chamber to conclude that Mr. Stanisic's and Mr. Simatovic's involvement in Bosnia went into a hiatus throughout this period -- I'm sorry, throughout this period they were very much involved in joint operations designed to hold onto the targeted lands they seized in 1992 and to resist the Bosnian government's attempts to recapture this land. You will hear summary evidence of the accused's involvement in Bosnia in the time between 1992 and 1995 primarily from a headquarters they established in Bajina Basta in Serbia, just across the border with Bosnia. I would now like to turn the attention of the Chamber to the crimes charged in the indictment related to Trnovo. The facts of what occurred in Srebrenica in July 1995 have been the subject of several trials in these courtrooms. I will not repeat them here; they are well known. We all know that the slaughter of the Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica marks the single, most egregious atrocity perpetrated against the Bosnian Muslim people. The two accused here in this trial are charged with the death of three men and three boys whose murder was captured on videotape. In order for you to understand the Prosecution's case as to why Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic are responsible for the deaths of the six, we must look at what is occurring in another part of the country prior to Srebrenica. I want to focus your attention on the north-west corner of Bosnia, shown here on slide 119, a place referred to as the Bihac pocket which in 1993 had a population of approximately 300.000 people, mostly Muslims. Its local leader, a Muslim man by the name of Fikret Abdic sought to extricate himself from the war in Bosnia by dissociating himself with the Bosnian government and entering into an uneasy alliance with Milosevic in Belgrade. So in October of 1993 Abdic traded his war with Croatia and Serbia for a war with his Bosniak brothers in Sarajevo, and shortly thereafter, the Bosnian army was engaging Abdic's poorly trained and equipped men. Abdic turned to Milosevic for help and within a short time Milosevic responded by sending Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic to the Bihac pocket to command an operation called Pauk, or the Spider. Milosevic sent the two men whom he could rely on for this task. Stanisic would in turn bring with him the men who he had come to rely on in his covert operations in the rest of Bosnia, the Special Units of the Serbian DB led by Colonel Bozovic, Legija, Captain Dragan, and Arkan. They established their headquarters in Mount Petrova Gora in the Krajina. The diary depicted here on slide 120 is one of the commanders in the Pauk operation and shows a number of references to Mr. Simatovic and one of several references to Mr. Stanisic. We can also find references to Mr. Stanisic in the recently acquired diary of Ratko Mladic from this period. On the 6th of April, 1995, Mladic met with General Perisic, Jovica Stanisic, and others in Belgrade to discuss the situation in Bihac. As shown here on slide 121, Jovica Stanisic described the support given to both Fikret Abdic and Milan Martic and more importantly said: "I sent 150 men from Slavonia through Pauk." The Special Units of the Serbian DB were to join forces with the Serbian Krajina army as well as Abdic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Two of the three tactical groups formed with these joint forces would be under the direct command of the Special Units of the Serbian DB. The second tactical group would be placed under Legija's command. And the third tactical group would be placed under the command of Colonel Rajo Bozovic. The Skorpions were part of Legija's tactical group. The Skorpions were first formed after the fall of Vukovar, following a request by the Djeletovci oil company to Milan Milovanovic, a minister of the SAO SBWS - its commander Slobodan Medic, also known as Boca. The unit's task was to protect the oil fields in the Djeletovci, a task at times shared with Arkan's men. The unit grew quickly to include several hundred men. The Serbian DB provided the Skorpions with significant equipment and paid the salaries of its members in cash. Approximately 30 per cent of its members had been trained in one of the Serbian DB training camps in Kula, Mount Tara, Lipovaca, and Golubic. Its members were also issued with identification papers, identifying them as Serbian DB members. Milanovic was the intermediary between Medic, Simatovic, and Stanisic. In 1996 after the war some members of the unit would remain in the service of the Serbian DB and join the JSO. The two men that you see in this video on slide 122 are Legija, who you have already heard much about, and Slobodan Medic, the man who gave the direct order to kill the six captives in Trnovo. The video is long and I will not ask the Chamber to look at all the relevant parts now, but in one segment you will hear Legija deciding what to do with captured Muslims. His decision, as you might expect, is consistent with his treatment of non-Serbs in other areas of the conflict. Mr. Simatovic would mention this involvement in Pauk in his May 1997 speech in Kula when he said: "In Western Bosnia, the unit was the backbone of Fikret Abdic's army." The Pauk operation lasted until August 1995. Let me now take you back to Eastern Bosnia, July of 1995. The Bosnian Serbs decided to overtake the UN protected area of Srebrenica. By the end of July, nearly 8.000 Muslim boys and men would be summarily executed. Not all of the murders were committed in the immediate vicinity of Srebrenica. In addition to their presence in the Bihac pocket, Special Units of the Serbian DB were also present in Central Bosnia. The story of the involvement of the Serbian DB in what happened in Srebrenica began about a month before the massacre. In late June the Serbian MUP was active in rounding up Serb men who were believed to be avoiding their military service. Slide 123 is a document recording this. Morale of the Serb soldiers at this stage was very low. There was a high incidence of desertion. Many of these men crossed into Serbia to stay with family or to hide among the crowds in Serbia's cities. In this particular document, Tomislav Kovac, the deputy minister, reports that on June 23rd he has handed over to the VRS in excess of 1.500 men taken into custody in Serbia and turned over to the RS MUP. Even with this operation to compel able-bodied men to go to the front lines in Bosnia, Mladic and Karadzic were still woefully in need of additional troops. In late June of 1995 a meeting was held at the MUP Serbia to decide upon a response to a request for assistance that had been made by the Government of Republika Srpska. In a meeting attended by Arkan and Slobodan Medic, the decision was taken that members of the Special Units of the Serbian DB under the command of a member, Vaso Mijovic, a senior commander in the Special Units, would go to Bosnia and help fight the Bosnian army. Only a few days later on the 30th of June, 1995, Slobodan Milosevic met with Ratko Mladic, Fikret Abdic, and Mile Mrksic in Belgrade. Also present was Milosevic's most trusted subordinate: Jovica Stanisic. Again, General Mladic made notes about this meeting. They discussed the support to be given to the Republika Srpska and Slobodan Milosevic specifically asked Stanisic to solve the logistic problems. In response, Jovica Stanisic proposed to send more men in addition to the men he had already provided; 80 men from Erdut, namely Arkan's men; and 80 men from Djeletovci, namely the Skorpions. Slide 124 shows an entry from Mladic's diary regarding this. I would now draw your attention to slide 125 and would like to return to a portion of the Skorpion videotape that shows their arrival on the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the religious ceremony I showed you at the start of this opening, a ceremony which took place in Djeletovci, this large group travelled to Pale in a Serb-controlled area just outside of Sarajevo. As you can see in the excerpt of a report at the bottom of slide 125, an RS MUP report records their arrival and their planned deployment to the Trnovo battle-field the next day. The map on slide 126 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The map on slide 126 shows the relationship between Pale, Trnovo, Sarajevo, and Jahorina. The ski resort in Jahorina was used as the command post. During the course of the trial you will get a sense of the size of this operation by seeing the many paramilitaries gathered in Jahorina. One of the ways we can track the presence of the Special Units of the Serbian DB is that they sustained significant and regular casualties in the Trnovo area. Slide number 127 shows a chart of some of the documents that the Prosecution will introduce establishing that throughout this period Special Units of the Serbian DB were present. Another senior member of the Special Units I would like to introduce you to is Vaso Mijovic. It was him that commanded the Special Units while they were operating in Trnovo. When Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July, a column of 10.000 to 15.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys fled. The column was hit by Bosnian Serb artillery on the 12th, and those who survived the artillery barrage, several thousand, were captured. These prisoners were systematically executed at a variety of places between the 13th and 17th of July, 1995. Some of the captured were distributed for execution outside the Srebrenica area. Approximately 15 captives were given to the Skorpions as their complement of detainees to be killed. Some of these prisoners were delivered to the Skorpions at their base in Trnovo. Slide 129 shows a report of Mijovic on the official letter-head of the Special Units of the Serbian DB, at this stage officially called the Unit for Anti- Terrorist Operations or JATD. On the 19th of July, Mijovic notifies his counterparts in the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs that he was ordered to pull back from the zone of combat to "undertake other assignments." What those assignments were the report does not say. We do know that this is around the period in which the six captives were killed. Slobodan Medic and a group of Skorpions put six of the captives in a truck and drove them to an isolated area near Trnovo to kill them. Medic ordered that what they were about to do be videotaped. Slide 130 contains a short excerpt of that video. It does not include the actual executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Skorpions shouted abuse at the prisoners, kicked them -- kicked them and taunted the youngest boy that he would die a virgin. The six almost certainly knew that they were about to die. They were made to wait while the truck driver went into town to get a newly charged battery for the camcorder. Once the camcorder was ready, four of the prisoners were made to stand in a line while the other two were forced to lay in the grass. The four standing up were then shot one by one. After the first was shot in the back, the others were made to walk to the spot where the previous victim had just fallen to stand and wait. As some of the victims twitched in the grass, additional shots were fired into their heads to ensure that they would not survive. The two who had been forced to lie in the grass were made to carry the bodies into a nearby house. The Skorpions then shot and killed the two remaining men. In this report of the 24th of July, 1995, shown on slide 131, we can tell by this rotation report that the Skorpions returned to their regular duties. Here the staff commanders remarks that the rotation of troops between the Banja Luka special police and the Skorpions has gone smoothly. It is the Prosecution's case, as summarised here on slide 132, that the Skorpions were one of the units of the Serbian DB and that the accused are criminally responsible for killing of the three men and three boys in Trnovo. In this case, these members of the units of the DB under the command of a senior DB officer, Vaso Mijovic, were made available to Karadzic, Mladic, and other core members of the joint criminal enterprise to perpetrate crimes in furtherance of their common criminal purpose. Around the same time-period, Arkan was in the municipality of Sanski Most. He was there primarily to frighten deserters from the Bosnian Serb army into holding the front lines against the Croatian forces who were by now re-taking some of the territory lost to the Serbs in 1992. We can see from this report in slide 134 that Mr. Stanisic is in direct contact with Arkan on these matters. While in the municipality of Sanski Most, a place that after 1992 had a few Muslims left, Arkan engaged once again in his characteristically brutal crimes. His presence there was part of a larger Serbian DB operation that encompassed not only Sanski Most but Mrkonjic Grad, Kljuc, and Prijedor. This coordinated mission involved the Special Units of the Serbian DB commanded by Rajo Bozovic; Arkan's Tigers were under his command. In mid-1995 advances by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina threatened to re-take Sanski Most from the Serbs. To prevent this, Arkan's Tigers were sent to Sanski Most. On the 19th of September, Arkan's men arrived in large numbers and rounded up any remaining Muslims they could find. They were imprisoned in the Hotel Sanus in appalling conditions, 30 of them were kept in the hotel's small boiler room, a room from which they were occasionally removed in order to be beaten. Two detainees died from this brutality. On September 20th, 1995, Arkan's Tigers took at least 12 men from the Hotel Sanus to a house in the nearby village. There the men were shot two at a time in the back of the head. The last two victims had their throats slashed when Arkan's men ran out of bullets. On the 21st of September, Arkan's Tigers took another group of approximately 65 Muslims where they were executed in a similar manner. Several days later several hundred Muslim detainees were placed on a bus and expelled from Sanski Most. One month later, on the 23rd of October, 1995, following the events in Sanski Most, Radovan Karadzic would publicly give an award to Arkan. He was now leaving Bosnia. His work now complete. It is ironic that his presence in Bosnia would end in front of the very town hall in Bijeljina where it had begun. I would turn your attention to slide number 135 while I play this video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "For the guard and for you as commander of the guard. "Thank you very much, Mr. President. "With a lot of gratitude for your presence here. It's not the end. This is -- "Thank you very much. Would you like to address the guard."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is the Prosecution's case -- it is the Prosecution's case that the accused are criminally responsible for the crimes committed in Sanski Most because Arkan was a co-member in the joint criminal enterprise and a member of the Serbian DB units. The accused provided Arkan with some of the support and military supplies he needed to perpetrate these crimes. It is also the Prosecution's theory that they are responsible, having made members of the Special Units of the Serbian DB available to other members of the joint criminal enterprise, in this case Radovan Karadzic, who directed them to perpetrate crimes in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. After NATO finally struck some Bosnian Serb positions, Mladic's troops took UN peacekeepers hostage in June 1995 and placed them as human shields on potential targets. Milosevic, immediately recognising the jeopardy this placed Serbia in before the international community sent Stanisic to intervene, to go with Simatovic, and with the full authority of Milosevic to return with the hostages unharmed. The Prosecution does not deny Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic any of the honour or respect they have earned and deserve in this display of courage, freeing the hostages and perhaps even saving their lives. Should the Court find them guilty of crimes after this trial, the Prosecution will join the Defence in submitting that their deeds during the hostage crisis merits consideration by the Chamber in assessing an appropriate sentence. It is the Prosecution's case, however - and there can be no mistake regarding this - the authority Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic commanded that day, the day they decided to use their authority and their ability to save lives, is tragically the very same authority and the very same ability that they had used more often over the prior four years to take lives, to persecute innocents, to drive people from their homes. The reason Mr. Milosevic sent them there during the hostage crisis, one of the most tense and volatile events during the war, when all the eyes of the world were fixed on what might happen to these UN peacekeepers, the reason he sent them there was because they, like no one else, had the capacity to walk in among this madness and come out with the hostages unharmed. I would like now to turn to the indictment itself and offer a brief explanation of the charges and the Prosecution's theory of the case. The indictment charges both accused with crimes against humanity in violation of Article 5 of the Tribunal's Statute and violations of the laws and customs of war, in violation of Article 3 of the Statute. Slide 137 is a summary of the indictment against Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic. The crimes against humanity are enumerated in Counts 1, 2, 4, and 5 of the indictment and are respectively: Count 1, the crime of persecution in violation of Article 5(h); Count 2, murder in violation of Article 5(a); Count 4, deportation in violation of 5(d); and finally forcible transfer, one of the inhumane acts prohibited under Article 5(i) of the Statute. The crime of murder is also charged as a violation of the laws and customs of war and it is charged in Count 3 which charges murder as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and punishable under Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute.
