It is the Prosecution's case that the accused are individually criminally responsible for these crimes pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute in that they participated in these crimes with the requisite intent in the following ways: They committed the crimes as members of and participated in a joint criminal enterprise whose goal and purpose was to perpetrate these crimes; they participated in the planning of these crimes; they ordered some of the crimes in this indictment; they aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, and execution of the crimes charged in this indictment. Further, that with the requisite mens rea they aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, and execution of the crimes. It is the Prosecution's case that both accused were part of and helped form a joint criminal enterprise, a criminal enterprise conceived at the highest levels of the Government of the Republic of Serbia along with core members from the affected regions in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, an enterprise that conceived of and implemented a criminal plan designed to secure exclusively for Serbs land lying in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. To acquire these targeted territories this criminal enterprise would envisage the large and rapid removal of the non-Serb population by the perpetration of the crimes of murder and persecution. Crimes of this magnitude are always the product of a collective, a large group of people who work together to realise their common criminal purpose. The intent to commit the crimes charged in this indictment can be found in all levels of the organisations that were involved in their commission. This case will focus on the highest echelon of those co-perpetrators, the most senior participants. It is the Prosecution's position that at all times relevant to this case these core members shared the intent to remove non-Serbs from designated parts of Croatia and Bosnia through murder and persecutory acts. The glue that bound them together, that harmonised their individual contributions, that ensured that they worked in unison toward a common goal was the shared criminal intent. The jurisprudence of joint criminal enterprise has evolved to recognise that such criminal enterprises may come to take several forms, as shown on slide number 140. These different forms reflect the nuances between the different ways in which co-perpetrators can join, conceive of, and implement their criminal plans. While the actus reus of each of these forms is essentially identical, they are distinguished based upon their mental element or mens rea. The evidence you will hear in this case is consistent with two forms of joint criminal enterprise. JCE 1, which is sometimes referred to as the basic form, conceives of criminal responsibility for members of a criminal enterprise engaged in a common criminal agreement to commit a specific crime. While each member may carry out a different role in the commission of the crime, they nonetheless each intend for that specific crime to be committed and contribute to it. This is to be contrasted with JCE 3, sometimes referred to as the extended form, in which the crime charged, while not part of the originally intended crime, is nonetheless a natural and foreseeable consequence of the implementation of that criminal purpose. With respect to this case, firstly, most importantly, and the principal legal theory of the Prosecution is that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic were members of the core group of co-perpetrators that conceived of the crimes contained in this indictment. At all times relevant to these charges they had the shared intent to forcibly remove non-Serbs from designated areas in an effort to effect fundamental demographic changes in the population. The intent that they shared was not only to forcibly remove these targeted groups of non-Serbs, but they shared the intent to kill them and to persecute them as a means to realise their goals. How do we know that they shared this intent? There will be much evidence from which the Chamber may conclude that the two accused shared the criminal intent of other core members such as Martic, Karadzic, Hadzic, Mladic. I will confine myself to a single example now. In Zvornik fighters belonging to Seselj, Arkan, and a group called the Yellow Wasps, the Vukovic brothers, were all engaged in the commission of serious crimes there. You will hear evidence that the Yellow Wasps were investigated by Mr. Stanisic, by the Serbian State Security, and subsequently arrested by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs. They were ultimately prosecuted in a Serbian court for crimes they committed in Bosnia and were sentenced to jail terms. While it was proper to investigate and arrest the Vukovic brothers, the question that is raised is: Why wasn't similar action taken against Seselj's men or Arkan's men? Not only was action not taken but you will be presented with evidence that the crimes they committed after Bijeljina and Zvornik were facilitated and supported by the two accused. It is the Prosecution's case that the only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn from this is that Arkan and Seselj were among -- that Arkan and Seselj were among the core members of the JCE and that Stanisic and Simatovic shared their intent to perpetrate the crimes in Zvornik. The evidence is also consistent with what is commonly referred to as joint criminal enterprise 3. The two accused as well as the other core members of the joint criminal enterprise shared the intent to forcibly remove non-Serbs from designated areas. Under this theory even absent a finding that the accused shared the intent to murder and persecute Muslim and Croats, they would remain liable if they shared the intent to forcibly remove these non-Serbs and they willingly accepted the proximate and foreseeable risk that this forcible removal of people would result in the commission of murders and persecutions. In the context of this case, the accused having joined with others possessing the shared intent of forcibly transferring people from their homes bear individual criminal responsibility for the crimes of persecution and murder which are reasonably foreseeable. The Prosecution will establish with compelling evidence that over the course of the duration of the joint criminal enterprise statements by other participants in the criminal plan and reports in the media of the notorious crimes made it abundantly clear to the two accused that the campaign of ethnic cleansing unleashed their plan -- unleashed by their plan involved the strong probability and in time the certainty that murder and persecution would result from it, and with that full awareness, they willingly proceeded knowingly assuming the risk that such grave crimes would occur. As I have previously said, the actus reus for JCE 1 and JCE 3 are, except for slight nuances --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. First, that there be a plurality of persons. Given the large collective nature of these crimes, we can in practical terms only identify for you and present evidence regarding those members we believe to be the core members of the joint criminal enterprise. These are the people indicated on the chart we have used several times over the course of this opening. The second actus reus element is the existence of a common purpose which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime under this Statute. It is the Prosecution's case that each of the crimes charged in this indictment was a purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. The third actus reus element is that the accused participate in furtherance of the common criminal design in a manner that assists in its achievement, contributes to it, materially helps its execution in a significant way. I will now in a very summary fashion using slide 143 to identify the acts of participation which the Prosecution allege incur criminal liability for Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, constantly the interpreters, both French and B/C/S, are approximately one or two lines behind. Give them an opportunity to take a breath now and then. That will certainly be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the Krajina, it is the Prosecution's case that their efforts to organise, finance, train, and equip Martic's men and army, thereby enabling them to perpetrate the serious crimes they did against the non-Serb population of the Krajina, was an act of participation in the overall joint criminal enterprise. Similarly, with respect to the SAO SBWS, it is the Prosecution's case that the accused's acts of participation in the joint criminal enterprise were in part financing and equipping Arkan and his men who directly perpetrated the crimes. With respect to both the Krajina and the SAO SBWS, Mr. Stanisic and Simatovic gave direction to the local political leaders, including Martic, Babic, and Hadzic to ensure that their political activities also advanced the goals of the common criminal purpose. Finally, even if after the conclusion of this case the Chamber has a reasonable doubt about whether Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic directly funded and equipped Arkan, you would still -- they would still be responsible for his crimes, the crimes of another co-member in a joint criminal enterprise, if the Chamber was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that they were in fact part of the same joint criminal enterprise. With respect to the Bosnian municipalities that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic had a role in their take-over in 1992, it is the Prosecution's contention that their culpable acts of participation in the JCE included: Planning the attacks; providing training, arms, equipment, and funding; and in some instances, they also arranged military transport for the direct perpetrators of the crimes. In the event the Chamber finds that the evidence does not permit an inference that they directed immediate perpetrators of these crimes and in fact that it was Bosnian Serb leaders alone who directed them to commit crimes, the Prosecution's case would be that placing these men and this equipment at the disposal of another core member of the JCE to use to advance the criminal purpose of the JCE also incurs liability. With respect to Trnovo, their acts of participation include deploying the Skorpions which, it is the Prosecution's case, were part of the Special Units. Also, if the evidence does not suggest that they personally knew of the killings of the six males, it is the Prosecution's case that by placing their men at the disposal of other members of the JCE, in this case Mladic and Karadzic, also incurs to them liability for the crimes they committed under the direction of these other core members. With respect to Sanski Most, as you request see on slide 145, the Prosecution's case is similar to our case with respect to other crimes perpetrated in Bosnia. Finally, Your Honours, in such a large collective crime, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in the Brdjanin appeal judgement recognised that those most responsible for these serious crimes are also those most removed from them. It considers that those high-level members of the enterprise can and do use others to directly perpetrate the crimes they intend, and as such bear individual criminal responsibility. Under this theory, the core members of the joint criminal enterprise, sharing a common intent to remove non-Serbs used others to directly advance their criminal goals. Those they used may or may not have also shared their intent, but this theory holds that even absent proof of a shared intent with these perpetrators, the accused are criminally responsible because they employed these people as instrumentalities of their criminal plan. To give you an example from this case, I remind you about what we have already said about Bosanski Samac. When it became necessary, Jovica Stanisic would personally intervene to have one of the primary perpetrators released, a man named Crni, so that he could return to Samac and continue his crimes. Did Crni and Stanisic share the same intent? Probably, but even absent a finding that they did share the same intent, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic bear responsibility for the crimes of Crni if the Court finds that Crni was used as an instrumentality of the joint criminal enterprise to perpetrate its objectives. It is the Prosecution's case that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic are responsible for and participated in the crimes charged in several ways as set out in the indictment and the pre-trial brief. It is not our case that each crime relied on only one mode of participation. Given the size of the Special Units and the breadth of Stanisic's and Simatovic's activities, it is most often the case that in any one criminal event their involvement in these crimes can be discerned in more than one way. The indictment also alleges that the two accused planned the crimes charged. It is the Prosecution's position that Stanisic's and Simatovic's establishment of 26 training camps, provision of instructors, supply of military weapons and logistical equipment to the direct perpetrators of the crimes is evidence upon which the Chamber could reasonably conclude they engaged in acts of planning as defined by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Chamber will recall slide number 42. In the Krajina, someone by the name of Milojevic referring to things going according to "training plan." You will also recall the statement of Vojislav Seselj in which he identifies Mr. Simatovic as the mastermind behind the plan for the take-over of Zvornik. Ordering. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, ordering concerns a person in a position of authority using that position to persuade another to commit an offence under the Statute. The order can be explicit or implicit and can be proved with circumstantial evidence. It is the Prosecution's case that the evidence will support a conclusion by the Chamber that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic sent Arkan to the several municipalities in the indictment where he committed crimes. And even if they did not explicitly tell him to commit the crimes of murder and persecution, in the context of their knowledge that everywhere he went he committed these crimes, the only conclusion that can be drawn is that their directing him to a particular location with a non-Serb population was an implied order to perpetrate the crimes of murder and persecution there. I will not spend any time discussing aiding and abetting at this stage. All of the acts the Prosecution attributes to Stanisic and Simatovic could be the basis of participation as an aider and abettor. Your Honours, in the indictment the Prosecution alleges that the accused committed these crimes by their acts and omissions. I would like to take just a few minutes to expound on what is meant by that phrase. The word "omission" actually has two distinct meanings according to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. One use of omission is as a form of criminal liability; the other use is a description of a factual situation from which inferences can be drawn. Omission as a legal form of ideal liability imagines a situation in which an accused has a legal duty toward the victim. For example, a legal duty to protect. It is not the Prosecution's case that Mr. Stanisic or Simatovic had an affirmative legal duty to ensure the welfare of the victims of crimes in Croatia and Bosnia. Omission as it applies to a factual determination from which inferences can be drawn is how the Prosecution uses the word "omission" in this case. For example, if over the course of this case the Chamber takes a view of the evidence that despite receiving information about the crimes which were being committed as a result of their contribution to the joint criminal enterprise and that in the face of that knowledge they failed to take any corrective measures such as instructing the members of the Special Units to refrain from criminal conduct, then the Court is entitled to draw the reasonable inference that such omission constituted encouragement, material support to the direct perpetrators of the crimes, because they were emboldened by the failure of Stanisic and Simatovic to take any corrective action. You have seen a video of Arkan on the veranda of his shop in the middle of Belgrade state publicly that he kills his prisoners. You will hear other evidence that he and his men were a regular sight in Belgrade. They moved openly, dressed in uniform, carrying military weapons, often in cars with tigers painted on the hood. His ability to travel freely around Belgrade under the nose of Stanisic, whose legal responsibility, if you recall, included the control of extremist groups; Arkan's confidence in his own impunity, a result of Mr. Stanisic's failure to ever take action against him, materially advanced the crimes Arkan committed in addition to the accused's positive acts of directing and supporting Arkan's crimes. Your Honours, this brings to a conclusion the Prosecution's summary of its evidence and overview of why it alleges that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic are criminally responsible for the crimes charged in the indictment. I thank you for your time and attention. As we prepare to call our first witness later this month, I give the Chamber as well as Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic my assurance and the assurance of Mr. Brammertz that the Prosecution will conduct its case according to the highest standards of fairness and justice, enabling this Chamber to reach a fair and just adjudication of the charges against the accused. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. There apparently was one contested issue. Mr. Jovanovic, I think it would be wise that -- one way or another that you agree with the Prosecution on what is still part of the indictment or not, and if it would assist you -- let me just have a look whether I still have it somewhere. In the decision, I think it was a decision of April 2007, wherein the ten incidents were struck and not to be led any evidence, there -- of course it clearly says that we still have Counts 1, 4, and 5 which are broader. So therefore -- and of course we find especially under 4 and 5 we have Bijeljina mentioned. So to say nothing in Bijeljina is part of the indictment anymore -- if that is your view, then I think we rather settle or come to conclusions in the beginning of the trial rather than at the end. I don't know whether you want to further discuss it with Mr. Groome and Ms. Brehmeier-Metz or -- at this moment the indictment is as it is, just I encourage and urge the parties to come at least to an understanding which is not so much apart from it. So I encourage you to understand that. And if any matter there remains, then perhaps it might be wise to address the Chamber in the early stages of the proceedings. Is there -- I was just wondering where exactly that was -- no, it's not on my screen anymore, but it's the second part of the decision. I don't know whether it was April or not, but the decision in which it's explained what it means that the ten incidents are taken out, whereas 18 remain, and there specific reference to the broader charges is made in that decision. This just as guidance for you. It will be quite a while before we resume. Is there any procedural matter that we need to address at this moment before we adjourn until the 29th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a matter I raised in an e-mail to your staff earlier today, but it would be helpful for the Chamber [sic] to have some idea about how the Chamber will calculate the amount of time allotted for cross-examination in the scheduling of witnesses. So if a witness were to take, let's say, an hour in examination-in-chief, if you could give us some idea about what the cross-examination time would be, it would be helpful to schedule the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time much depends in that respect on whether it's a 92 bis witness, whether it's a 92 ter statement, or whether it's a viva voce witness because that makes quite a difference, but we'll pay attention to it and we'll try to give you the guidance you're asking for. It sometimes also depends on the subject matter of the testimony. If it's highly contested, then of course there might be a request for more time for cross-examination, whereas if it is crime base and only contested at a certain level, it might be different. But we'll try to assist you as good as we can. Any other matter? Ms. Brehmeier-Metz.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour had requested me to find out about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, about the Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: -- the Deutschemarks of the number that was mentioned on one of the slides, slide 61, and I'm happy to say that after quite a bit of calculating I have come up with two numbers that I can give to Your Honours. Apparently at that point in time in late 1991, there were an official currency rate and a kind of semi-official currency rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: The official one was 1 Deutschemark amounting to 13 dinars, which would calculate the number given on the slide to approximately 93 million Deutschemarks. And the semi-official currency rate was 33.5 dinars, which would make approximately 36 million Deutschemarks. And all of that related to old Yugoslav dinars and not the new ones that were later established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So anything around 50 million Deutschemarks. That's -- thank you for that information. Any matter? Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I rise really to deal with the issue of Rule 84. I don't know if Your Honours would wish us to indicate for the record that we elect not to make an opening statement at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding. From informal communication with the parties, it appeared that neither Defence would like to make an opening statement, which means you still have an opportunity to make an opening statement after the Prosecution's case has been closed. And if there's any need to hear a Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. And may I also for the record indicate that the accused elects not a make an 84 bis statement for the same reasons that he elects not to go to the video conferencing room. I thought for -- out of an abundance of caution I should put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say it goes almost without saying because if we have no possibility to hear him, then of course he never could address the Chamber and that is the situation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's no other matter. Mr. Jovanovic, the Chamber understood that you also would not use the right to make an opening statement at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. In the informal communication while we were still discussing the schedule, the Defence has informed both the OTP and the Chamber that at this point in time the accused will not be giving a statement, and there will be no opening statement either for different reasons than those given by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. That is our position at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For you, the same applies, that you can make an opening statement at a later stage. Then still to be seen whether it would be at the same time for both Defence cases or one at the beginning of the presentation of one Defence case and the other at the beginning of the other, that's still to be seen. But at this moment there is no opening statement nor is there an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis. Which means that we adjourn and we will resume on Monday, the 29th of June, at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, I.
